title: The Vector Space Model
text: The vector space model represents every document in a collection as a point in a multidimensional space whose axes are the terms of the dictionary. A document becomes a vector of term weights, and a query is converted into a vector over the same dictionary, so that the two can be compared directly. Similarity between a document and a query is measured as the cosine of the angle between their vectors, which has the useful property of being independent of document length: a long document does not outrank a short one merely by containing more words. Ranking the collection by descending cosine similarity produces an ordered result list rather than the unordered set that a boolean retrieval strategy returns. The model was introduced in the SMART retrieval system and remains the conceptual foundation of most modern ranking functions, including the probabilistic and learned rankers that superseded it in raw effectiveness.

title: Inverted Index Structures
text: An inverted index is the data structure that makes term-based retrieval fast. For each term in the dictionary it stores a postings list naming every document that contains the term, usually together with the term frequency and sometimes the positions of each occurrence. Answering a query means intersecting or merging the postings lists of the query terms rather than scanning the collection, which turns a linear pass over every document into a lookup proportional to the number of matching documents. Postings lists are normally stored in document order so they can be merged in a single pass, and compressed with variable byte or delta encoding because the gaps between document identifiers are small. Storing positions enables phrase and proximity queries and lets a search engine build query-biased snippets, at the cost of roughly one integer per token in the collection.

title: Term Weighting with TF-IDF
text: Term weighting assigns each term in a document a number reflecting how well that term describes the document. The term frequency component rewards terms that occur often in the document, while the inverse document frequency component penalises terms that occur in many documents of the collection. Inverse document frequency is computed as the logarithm of the collection size divided by the number of documents containing the term, so a term appearing in every document receives a weight of zero and contributes nothing to ranking. Multiplying the two components gives the familiar TF-IDF weight. Dividing each weight by the Euclidean norm of the document's weight vector normalises for length, which prevents long documents from dominating the ranking simply because their raw term counts are larger. The choice of logarithm base rescales every weight by the same constant and therefore does not affect the ranking at all.

title: Okapi BM25
text: BM25 is a probabilistic ranking function that estimates the probability that a document is relevant to a query. It refines TF-IDF in two ways. First, term frequency is saturated: the contribution of a term grows quickly for the first few occurrences and then levels off, controlled by the parameter k1, on the reasoning that a document mentioning a term twenty times is not twice as relevant as one mentioning it ten times. Second, document length is normalised against the average length of the collection, with the parameter b controlling how aggressively long documents are penalised. Typical settings are k1 near 1.2 and b near 0.75. BM25 consistently outperforms unmodified TF-IDF cosine similarity on standard test collections and remains a strong baseline that neural retrieval systems are still measured against.

title: Latent Semantic Analysis
text: Latent semantic analysis applies a truncated singular value decomposition to the term-document matrix of a collection, factoring it into a lower-dimensional space of latent concepts. Documents that share no vocabulary can end up close together in this reduced space if they use different words for the same idea, which partially addresses the synonymy problem that defeats a purely lexical vector space model. The decomposition also provides a natural way to visualise a collection: projecting documents onto the first two or three singular vectors places them on a plane or in a volume that can be plotted directly, with the retained singular values indicating how much of the original variance survives the projection. The cost is interpretability, since the latent dimensions do not correspond to any nameable concept, and computation, since the decomposition is collection-wide work that must be repeated when the collection changes.

title: Evaluating Retrieval Quality
text: Retrieval quality is measured against a test collection of queries paired with relevance judgments. Precision is the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant and recall the fraction of relevant documents that were retrieved; because a system can trade one against the other, they are normally reported together or combined into the harmonic mean known as the F measure. Precision at a fixed cutoff reflects what a user actually sees on the first page of results, while average precision summarises the whole ranking by averaging the precision observed at each relevant document. Since no single query is representative, metrics are averaged over many queries, and the eleven-point interpolated precision-recall graph plots the trade-off across the full recall range. Judgments are typically gathered by pooling the top results of every participating system, because exhaustively judging a large collection is infeasible.

title: Relevance Feedback and Query Expansion
text: Relevance feedback improves a query using evidence about which returned documents the user considered useful. The Rocchio algorithm implements this in the vector space model by moving the query vector toward the centroid of the documents marked relevant and away from the centroid of those marked irrelevant, weighted by three coefficients that control how much the original query, the positive examples and the negative examples each contribute. The reformulated query typically contains far more terms than the original, which improves recall by matching documents that use related vocabulary, and the effect is usually visible after a single round. Pseudo-relevance feedback applies the same arithmetic without asking the user anything, simply assuming that the top few results are relevant; it helps on average but can fail badly when the initial ranking is poor, a failure mode known as query drift.

title: Web Crawler Architecture
text: A web crawler discovers documents by fetching pages and following their links. It maintains a frontier of URLs still to be visited, normally a priority queue ordered so that shallower and more important pages are fetched first. Politeness is essential: a crawler must consult the robots exclusion file of each host before requesting a path, honour any crawl delay the host declares, and limit how many concurrent connections it opens to a single server. Duplicate detection operates at two levels, since exact duplicates are caught by hashing the normalised content while near duplicates, such as the same article behind different tracking parameters, require a similarity fingerprint like simhash and a comparison by Hamming distance. Extraction then strips navigation, advertising and other boilerplate to recover the main text worth indexing.

title: The Robots Exclusion Protocol
text: The robots exclusion protocol lets a site tell automated clients which parts of it they may fetch. A plain text file at the root of the host lists user agent groups, each followed by allow and disallow rules matched against the path of a request. The protocol is advisory rather than enforced, so compliance is a matter of good behaviour rather than access control, and a file that cannot be fetched is conventionally treated as permitting the crawl. Many hosts also publish a crawl delay directive expressing the minimum interval they want between requests, and a sitemap reference pointing at a machine-readable list of their canonical URLs. Because parsing the file for every request would be both slow and impolite, a crawler caches the parsed rules per host for the duration of a crawl.

title: Full Text Search in PostgreSQL
text: PostgreSQL provides full text search through the tsvector and tsquery types. A tsvector holds the normalised lexemes of a document together with their positions, produced by a text search configuration that applies a stemmer and removes stop words for a particular language. Storing a tsvector in a generated column keeps it consistent with the source text automatically, and a GIN index over that column makes matching a tsquery fast enough for interactive use. Ranking is available through functions that weight matches by frequency and by position, allowing title matches to count for more than body matches. The result is a capable search facility inside the database, which avoids operating a separate search server, though it offers less control over the weighting scheme than an application-level implementation of a specific retrieval model.
